hero.exampleTitle: One button, one tagged HTTP request

problem.heading: Prevent duplicate HTTP requests from repeat clicks in Angular
problem.intro: A user can click Save twice before the first POST completes. Two requests may then update the same record, while a manual loading flag can miss an error or a follow-up GET. This guide shows the button-level problem, a simple boolean approach, and how ngx-request-lock ties a button to selected HttpClient calls. Server-side idempotency is still needed for operations that must never run twice.

symptoms.title: Signs your Angular UI is out of sync with HTTP
symptoms.list:
• Duplicate POST/PUT/DELETE requests from repeated interactions.
  • Follow-up refresh calls racing the mutation they reflect.
  • Related actions (Save + Reset, Submit + Refresh) remaining clickable during active requests.
  • Ad hoc loading booleans scattered across components.
  • Loading flags stuck at true when an error path skips resetting them.
  • Disabled state logic drifting out of sync with the HTTP request lifecycle.

naive.title: Why a single loading boolean breaks down
naive.text: Toggling component-level booleans works for single requests, but degrades quickly as complexity grows. Sequential refreshes, related actions, or panel states require separate flags that must be manually reset on every error path

withLibrary.title: Lock the button with ngx-request-lock
withLibrary.text: Tag each relevant request with the same requestId through HttpContext. The interceptor counts pending calls per ID and the directive disables linked buttons. It releases them after success, error or cancellation, subject to a 10-second safety timeout. This limits repeat clicks in the browser; it does not deduplicate requests already sent.

scope.title: What this library does not do
scope.list:
• Does not cancel or debounce requests.
  • Does not replace server-side HTTP idempotency.
  • Does not provide global spinners or toast notifications.

architecture.heading: How an Angular HTTP interceptor tracks button loading state
architecture.intro: ngx-request-lock links selected HttpClient calls to buttons through four Angular primitives: an HttpContextToken, a functional interceptor, a signal service and a directive. The same requestId groups related calls. See when the counter starts, ends and updates the UI.

buildingBlocks.title: HttpContext, interceptor, signal and directive
buildingBlocks.list:
• REQUEST_LOCK_ID: an HttpContextToken<string | null> that tags a request with a lock identifier. Multiple requests can share the same ID to form a single flow.
  • createRequestLockContext(id): constructs the HttpContext attached to the request. A click handler can use the ready context on RequestLockMouseEvent instead.
  • requestLockInterceptor: functional interceptor that reads the ID from the context and updates the service.
  • RequestLockService: singleton service holding a reference-counted map of pending requests, exposed via the boolean signal isPending(id). Any component can consume this signal to render custom in-flight states.
  • RequestLockDirective ([ngxRequestLock]): attaches to any element containing or matching a <button>, enriches its native click event with requestId and HttpContext, observes isPending(requestId), and updates the disabled attribute. All instances sharing a requestId lock and unlock together.
  • provideRequestLock(): registers provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([requestLockInterceptor])) in a single call.

dataFlow.title: From a button click to an HTTP response
dataFlow.clickDescription: The directive disables the clicked button and exposes its request ID.
dataFlow.contextDescription: HttpClient carries the ID in client-side HttpContext metadata.
dataFlow.interceptorDescription: The interceptor starts tracking, forwards the call and decrements on finalize.
dataFlow.signalDescription: The pending signal updates every button sharing that ID.
dataFlow.caption: The signal feeds back to the buttons. A 10-second safety timeout can release a button before a slow request ends.
dataFlow.diagramAriaLabel: Request lock data flow diagram: user actions drive directive instances and HTTP requests through the interceptor and RequestLockService
dataFlow.steps:
• A user action initiates the flow. Directives bound to the flow's requestId set isBlocked = true and disable the button. When the click binding is on the directive host, the event also receives the generated requestId and ready HttpContext.
  • The application sends HTTP requests whose HttpContext includes the requestId, either from event.context or via createRequestLockContext(id). Follow-up refreshes or chained calls can reuse the same ID.
  • For each request, requestLockInterceptor reads REQUEST_LOCK_ID, calls RequestLockService.start(id), and appends finalize(() => end(id)). The service reference-counts pending requests per ID.
  • isPending(id) remains true until every request with that ID completes. Directives and wrappers unblock only when all calls settle.
  • Two safety timeouts unblock the directive: at 500 ms if no requests are tracked, and at 10 s as an unconditional ceiling.

architecture.httpContextNote: HttpContext is local. HttpContext holds client-side Angular request metadata. It is never serialized to headers, body, or query params, and never reaches the server

refCount.title: Why concurrent requests need a counter
refCount.text: RequestLockService increments a counter per ID on start and decrements it on end. Concurrent calls can keep isPending(id) true until the final call settles. The directive also has an unconditional 10-second safety unlock, so a slow request may outlast the disabled state.
refCount.note: RequestLockService.isPending(id) returns a new computed signal on each call. Assign the returned signal to a property if reading it repeatedly within the same component

installation.intro: Install ngx-request-lock in an Angular 22+ app, register its functional HTTP interceptor, and add ngxRequestLock to a button. The first example passes the click event’s HttpContext to HttpClient; later sections show shared IDs and existing interceptor setups.

requirements.title: Requirements
requirements.list:
• Angular v22 or newer, declaring peer dependencies @angular/common and @angular/core at ^22.0.0.
  • Standalone APIs, functional HTTP interceptors, and signals enabled (default in v22).
  • The default ID generator uses crypto.randomUUID(), requiring a secure browser context (HTTPS or localhost).

install.title: Install ngx-request-lock with npm
install.text: Install the package from npm. No runtime dependencies exist other than tslib
install.peerNote: The library ships as an Angular Package Format build, supports tree-shaking, and sets sideEffects: false

provider.title: Register the Angular HTTP interceptor
provider.text: provideRequestLock() is an environment provider factory that registers the functional interceptor. Add it to the providers array in ApplicationConfig
provider.warning: Do not call provideHttpClient() separately alongside provideRequestLock(). The factory includes provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([requestLockInterceptor])) internally. Calling provideHttpClient(...) again in the same providers array overrides it, disabling the interceptor

manualProvider.title: Manual registration
manualProvider.text: If the application configures provideHttpClient with existing interceptors, omit provideRequestLock() and register requestLockInterceptor directly
manualProvider.note: The interceptor is a plain HttpInterceptorFn. Its execution order matches its position in withInterceptors(...)

context.title: Attach the lock ID to the request
context.text: The interceptor processes only requests carrying a value under REQUEST_LOCK_ID in their HttpContext. Use createRequestLockContext(id) to build this context
context.bullets:
• REQUEST_LOCK_ID is an HttpContextToken<string | null> defaulting to null.
  • createRequestLockContext(id) returns an HttpContext with the specified token. If id is falsy, an empty context is returned and the interceptor skips the request.
  • Untracked HTTP requests pass through unmodified.

directive.title: Disable a button with ngxRequestLock
directive.text: RequestLockDirective is a standalone directive with selector [ngxRequestLock] and exportAs: 'requestLock'. Import it into the component's imports array and apply it to target elements
directive.bullets:
• Each directive instance generates a unique requestId via crypto.randomUUID(). Bind [requestId] explicitly to share an ID across multiple elements and coordinate a flow.
  • Export the instance via #lock="requestLock" to read lock.requestId() for single-element locks. For shared flows, manage the ID in the component (e.g., signal(crypto.randomUUID())) and bind it to directives and createRequestLockContext(...) calls.
  • The directive locates the button via elementRef.closest('button') or the first child <button>, toggling its disabled attribute. Non-button host elements receive no DOM modifications, but their lock state still updates the shared signal for wrapper components.

lifecycle.title: How the UI unlocks
lifecycle.text: UI unlocking occurs automatically as HTTP request lifecycles complete
lifecycle.steps:
• On click, the directive disables the associated button.
  • requestLockInterceptor finds the ID in HttpContext and calls RequestLockService.start(id). Its finalize handler decrements on success, error or cancellation.
  • RequestLockService keeps a signal<Map<string, number>> and exposes isPending(id).
  • The directive observes that signal and re-enables its button when the count returns to zero, or after its 10-second safety timeout.

safety.title: Safety timeouts
safety.text: Two timeouts prevent elements from staying disabled indefinitely:
safety.bullets:
• 500 ms: unblocks the directive if no pending HTTP requests are detected (handling actions that fire no network calls).
  • 10 s: unconditional ceiling that unlocks elements if requests hang.

shared.tipConfig: Snippets assume provideRequestLock() is registered in app.config.ts (see the Installation page)

directiveUsage.heading: Disable an Angular button while an HTTP request runs
directiveUsage.intro: Add ngxRequestLock to a button, then pass the click event’s context or createRequestLockContext(id) to HttpClient. The directive disables the button until the tagged call settles, with a 10-second safety unlock. Try the live examples for save, delete, form submit and loading labels. For several related calls, see coordinating Angular HTTP flows.

nativeClick.title: Pass the request context through $event
nativeClick.text: The directive enriches the native click event with the generated requestId and a ready-to-use HttpContext, so the handler needs no template reference or manual context creation
nativeClick.bullets:
• Type the handler parameter as RequestLockMouseEvent.
  • Use event.context directly in the HttpClient request.
  • This works when the (click) binding is on the element carrying ngxRequestLock.

basic.title: One button and one HTTP request
basic.text: Minimal setup for a single interaction: element, directive, template reference requestLock, and an HTTP request using createRequestLockContext(id)
basic.bullets:
• #lock="requestLock" exposes the directive instance to the template.
  • lock.requestId() provides a stable UUID for the instance.
  • The button remains disabled until the tagged HTTP request settles, or until the 10-second safety timeout.

crud.title: Save, delete, and form examples
crud.text: The pattern applies to any HTTP action by changing the verb and payload while keeping the directive, exported reference, and context helper identical

directiveUsage.formNote: For a form submit button, keep validation and pending state in the same [disabled] expression when needed. The directive also writes the button’s native disabled attribute, so verify your form’s validation state after each request; it does not disable the whole form or stop submissions made outside this button.

pending.title: Show a loading label or spinner on the button
pending.text: To update labels or display spinners during request execution (e.g., swapping Save to Saving...), use the reactive signal provided by the service. Read RequestLockService.isPending(lock.requestId()) inside a computed() signal to update template state
pending.bullets:
• viewChild.required(RequestLockDirective) accesses the directive instance from the component class.
  • computed(() => service.isPending(lock().requestId)()) converts service state into a boolean signal.
  • Use @if (isPending()) in the template to swap labels or icons without managing manual loading flags or finalize callbacks.
  • Set [attr.aria-busy] during active requests to inform assistive technologies.
pending.tip: DOM button disabling by the directive and visual indicator updates via signals operate independently

custom.title: Custom directive: loading animation
custom.text: RequestLockDirective only toggles the native disabled attribute on target buttons. To add custom spinners or animations, extend the directive and override setBlockStatus
custom.info: In the documentation app, this implementation lives at src/app/pages/examples/loading-request-lock.directive.ts, kept separate from the core package to remain styling-agnostic
custom.usageText: Usage matches the base directive; only the selector and exported name change
custom.warning: Dependency injection and click host bindings (declared in host) are defined on the parent class. Do not shadow onClick or re-declare click bindings in the subclass; override setBlockStatus only

flowLock.heading: Coordinate Angular form buttons across chained HTTP requests
flowLock.intro: Give related buttons and HttpClient calls one requestId. A POST can start a follow-up GET while the same signal reports the flow as pending. The directive disables linked buttons until tracked calls settle, subject to its 10-second safety timeout. For a single button, see the Angular button examples.

sharedFlow.title: Share one requestId across buttons and requests
sharedFlow.text: Bind the same ID to primary actions, secondary actions, and follow-up refreshes to synchronize their disabled states
sharedFlow.tip: Store the ID in the component (e.g., signal(crypto.randomUUID())) and pass it to each [requestId] and createRequestLockContext(...) call. Regenerate the ID only when starting a new flow
sharedFlow.bullets:
• Multiple ngxRequestLock instances with the same ID share one pending-request count.
  • Follow-up HTTP calls tagged with that ID keep the buttons locked while they are pending, subject to the 10-second safety unlock.
  • The interceptor decrements the count on completion, error or cancellation.
  • For a form or panel, bind isPending(id) to visual state such as aria-busy; the directive itself disables buttons only.

formRefresh.title: Form example: POST followed by GET refresh
formRefresh.text: Tag the POST and its follow-up GET with the same requestId. The Save and Refresh buttons observe one pending counter. If requests last beyond 10 seconds, the directive’s safety timeout can re-enable the buttons before the HTTP flow completes.

inFlight.title: Whole-flow visual state
inFlight.text: A shared requestId can also drive container-level visual states (dimmed panels, overlays, or aria-busy regions) by reading RequestLockService.isPending(flowId)
inFlight.bullets:
• Containers do not require ngxRequestLock; they consume the pending signal directly.
  • Class bindings ([class.opacity-60]) manage visuals, while [attr.aria-busy] notifies assistive tech.
  • Container styling and button disabling stay synchronized through the shared signal.
  • This pattern complements per-button locking for comprehensive interface management.
inFlight.note: The directive does not style or modify non-button elements; container visuals are an application-level pattern

why.title: Key benefits
why.intro: The three core primitives (ngxRequestLock, a shared requestId, and createRequestLockContext) handle both isolated interactions and complex multi-request flows:
why.bullets:
• Shared button state: one requestId links several buttons to the same pending counter.
  • Fewer manual flags: the service exposes a signal for the calls you tag through HttpContext.
  • Error and cancellation handling: the interceptor decrements the count through finalize.
  • Safety bound: the directive re-enables buttons after 10 seconds even if a request is still pending; handle longer operations separately.
  • Custom visuals: a component can use isPending(id) for a panel or spinner; the directive itself only disables buttons.
